prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms, which brought time and frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level and opened a regime for tests of gravity, many-body physics and fundamental constants

statement.case_for: After the full exchange I keep optical lattice clocks (Katori, Ye) as a single prize part. The decisive physical step that answers the chair's novelty question is Katori's magic-wavelength lattice: it cancels the light shift while confining thousands of atoms in the Lamb-Dicke regime, which removes the Doppler and recoil limits of single-ion clocks and replaces the one-ion statistics of 2012 with massive parallel interrogation. That is a different physical idea from the frequency comb of 2005, which is the ruler that reads out any optical clock, and from the ion control of 2012. It is also what opened new physics: comparison of clocks at the millimetre scale tests gravitational redshift, interactions inside a degenerate Fermi gas of atoms in the clock (Ye's many-body programme) now matter at the 1e-19 level, and bounds on varying constants and ultralight dark matter come from these systems. Independent laboratories (Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE, and others) agree at the 1e-18 level, so maturity and reproducibility are as good as any candidate on the list. Five of eight of us converged on the same pair and the same division of credit, but I rest on the physics and not on the count. The citation should name magic-wavelength trapping so that it cannot be read as a second comb prize.
statement.case_against: The objection I take most seriously is the one Mehlig and Danielsson press: this is a measurement instrument in a lineage the Academy rewarded in 2005 and 2012, and a committee that weights fundamental importance above attribution could prefer the Higgs. The second objection is credit. I cannot verify from the files in this round whether Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Oates, Hinkley and others hold priority claims that would break a two-name prize, and the chair is right that this should be checked before the ballot. Third, the redefinition of the second has not happened, so the best-known application remains prospective, although the discovery content (new regime of precision, new physics tests) does not depend on it.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B031 eighth as metrology that refines a measurement line already honoured in 2005 and 2012, and prefers twisted bilayer graphene for its understood mechanism and quick replication.
responses.response: The chair asked whether novelty is your only objection, and I think your argument is the strongest one against my choice, so I will answer on substance. I accept that a clock which only improved the uncertainty of an existing scheme would not deserve a prize. What differs here is the trapping idea: a magic wavelength makes a many-atom sample as insensitive to its trap as a single isolated ion, and that is a new mechanism, not an increment, much as you would distinguish a new band structure from a cleaner sample. It also gave access to physics a single-ion clock cannot reach, namely millimetre-scale redshift and many-body interaction shifts in the clock itself. I also accept your standard of an understood mechanism and note that the clock meets it better than B024 does: every systematic shift is understood and budgeted. If B031 is not your first choice, I would like to know whether you could accept it as a second choice, because the two camps look closer in maturity terms than in novelty terms.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers the Higgs discovery with ATLAS and CMS as the most fundamental and best-confirmed result, and argues that clean attribution should not outweigh fundamental importance.
responses.response: I agree that the Higgs is the most important single result on the list, and I would not argue otherwise; I ranked it fourth only because of my deference on particle physics and the attribution problem. But the prize question is not which result is biggest, it is which result can be credited to at most three living people in a way that the community accepts. You propose Gianotti, Jenni and Della Negra, while others including Kroll and Lindroth would pick differently and Virdee is left out; the chair notes that no member has stated a rule that selects between founders and 2012 spokespeople. If you can state such a rule, that is the thing that would move me toward B005 and I would give it real weight, which is why I keep it as an alternative. Without that rule I think a prize that omits half of the CMS leadership would damage a result that deserves better. On the novelty point, I accept that the clock extends a lineage but I do not think that disqualifies it, since the lattice scheme opened regimes the earlier prizes did not.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers twisted bilayer graphene, arguing that independent replication and an explanatory continuum theory are enough maturity and that the 2018 experiment was the decisive step.
responses.response: Your request for a concrete maturity criterion is fair. By replication and by the flat-band picture, B024 passes. Where I still differ is the superconducting phase and the credit: the paper that made the field is the 2018 pair of experiments, and the first experimental author is not among the three names, so a three-name prize built on Bistritzer, MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero credits the theory fully and the experiment partly. Mehlig and you propose adding Bistritzer rather than the first author, which makes this sharper. I would be comfortable with B024 in a later year if that gap is resolved, and I have moved it from sixth to my first alternative because your argument about opening a new class of correlated matter is more persuasive to me than it was in round 1.

responses.point: Kroll supports B031 but asks that the priority claims of other lattice-clock groups and the pending redefinition of the second be weighed explicitly.
responses.response: I agree that the two issues you raised should be settled in the discussion and not left as footnotes. On priority, my reading is that Katori's proposal and first demonstration and Ye's accuracy and many-body programme are the decisive threads, and the others you name confirmed and extended them, but I flag that I cannot verify this myself and that the chair has asked for a check. On the redefinition of the second, I would not wait for it: Nobel prizes reward the discovery and it is already established, as with the comb prize, which preceded the practical uses by years. I would not change the configuration for either point unless the priority check shows that a third name is truly decisive.

uncertainties: Whether the priority record of Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Oates, Hinkley and others is compatible with a two-name prize; I cannot check this from the material available in this round.

Whether the committee regards a magic-wavelength lattice as distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, which Mehlig and Danielsson doubt; I think it is, but the judgement is partly about taste in what counts as a new regime.
I defer to colleagues on the Higgs attribution and on moire materials; a rule for choosing among Gianotti, Jenni, Della Negra and Virdee could change my ordering of B005.
Whether to treat the unresolved redefinition of the second as a reason to wait, which I do not.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with B031 (Katori, Ye). I have no personal tie to either laureate, and the recommendation in round 1 stands. As disclosed before, I have a possible connection to B016 (circuit QED: Blais, Wallraff, Schoelkopf) through my field, WACQT and Chalmers colleagues in superconducting circuits, and I would recuse myself or defer on B016 if the committee moves toward it. I also note that WACQT is linked to Lund quantum sensing and that Per Delsing, a Chalmers colleague, is not among the shortlisted names.
